title: Looped Weight-Space Programming: LLM-Written Transformers
author: ahmedheaklwsp

excerpt: Deep learning models normally get their weights from training. Once a transformer is trained, though, it is nothing more than a program written in matrices. If you know the program you want, you can skip training and write the matrices yourself. People have done this by hand for small problems (related work). Compilers such as Tracr go further, turning short programs into transformer weights automatically. Recently, Weight-Space Programming (Takehi, Teoh, Zhang and Khattab, MIT CSAIL) showed that a frontier LLM can edit a model's weights directly, without any training, and Fan et al. then had an open model rewrite its weights to fix its mistakes. Other groups have gone further and had LLMs set every weight of a tiny transformer, but only for toy tasks (Singh, AdderBoard). In those transformers, every step of a computation takes a separate block. Scaling one up to a hard problem would mean a far bigger transformer and a far bigger Claude bill, since Claude would have to write every one of those extra weights. We wanted to know whether LLM-written weights hold up on problems that need long chains of reasoning. Our main test is Maze-Hard, a benchmark of 30×30 mazes whose shortest paths run longer than 110 steps. Frontier LLMs struggle with it. For example, when Claude Opus 5.5 is asked for the shortest path, it solves only 26% of the test mazes it is given [1]. So instead of asking Claude to solve the mazes, we asked it to write a looped transformer that solves them, setting every weight by hand. The transformer has a single block with 19,936 weights. This block runs in a loop. Each forward pass moves a shortest-path search one step further, so the transformer keeps feeding the maze back through the same block until the path is complete. With enough passes, it solves 100% of the test mazes. That is more than the newest looped models trained for this benchmark reach.
